c.tagline: Argentina's high-altitude wine capital at the foot of the Andes.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis and remises are metered and cheap; radio taxis and apps (Uber, Cabify, DiDi) are widely used and often cheaper for airport runs.

emergency.note: Dial 911 for police and general emergencies; 107 is the ambulance/medical line and 100 is the fire brigade.

hood_landmark.Chacras de Coria: Chacras de Coria plaza, Luján de Cuyo

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around Plaza Independencia and the bus terminal; caution in Parque San Martín at night

hood_desc: The walkable heart around Plaza Independencia and the pedestrianised Sarmiento avenue, lined with cafés, wine bars and plane-tree-shaded plazas; the easiest base for first-time visitors.

The city's historic birthplace around Pedro del Castillo square, home to the Área Fundacional Museum and the ruins of colonial Mendoza; quiet, atmospheric and steeped in the city's earthquake history.
A leafy, upscale residential district beside the huge Parque General San Martín, good for joggers, families and travellers who want green space and calm a short walk from downtown.
A bohemian wine village in Luján de Cuyo just south of the city, known for its Sunday antiques fair, leafy plaza, boutique bodegas and a lively weekend bar-and-restaurant scene.
A busy adjoining suburb with the Palmares shopping-and-dining strip and easy Metrotranvía access; a good-value, local-feeling base with plenty of restaurants and nightlife.

water.note: Andes-fed tap water is safe to drink, though many visitors prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:30 AM to midnight; the Metrotranvía light rail runs about 6 AM to 11 PM with reduced weekend service.
transit.pay: Fares are paid with the rechargeable RedBus/SUBE contactless card (most buses no longer take cash); tap on boarding. Cards are sold at kiosks and terminals.
transit.note: Greater Mendoza is served by the MendoTran bus network and a single north–south Metrotranvía light-rail line linking Las Heras, the city centre, Godoy Cruz and Maipú.

food.name: Asado
food.desc: Beef grilled slowly over wood embers: vacio, costillas, chorizo and morcilla, brought to the table in waves with chimichurri.

places.name: Don Mario
places.note: Long-established parrilla locals name first, with generous classic cuts and good service.

places.name: El Palenque
places.note: Bustling pulperia-style spot on the bar street; simple grilled plates and jugs of wine.

places.name: Siete Cocinas
places.note: Regional Argentine kitchen treating Andean cuts and wood-fire cooking seriously.

food.name: Empanadas mendocinas
food.desc: Baked, not fried: hand-cut beef with onion, mild pepper, olives and boiled egg, sometimes raisins, sealed in a rope-edged repulgue.

places.name: El Palenque
places.note: Known for hearty homemade empanadas eaten standing at the bar with a Malbec.

places.name: Fuente y Fonda
places.note: Home-cooking dining room doing family-sized criollo plates including empanadas.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Historic covered market with counters baking empanadas through the morning.

food.name: Humita en chala
food.desc: Fresh corn mashed with onion, squash and cream, wrapped in the husk and steamed. A summer Andean staple served with cheese or a little sugar.

places.name: Siete Cocinas
places.note: Menu organised by Argentine region, so Cuyo classics like humita are done properly.

places.name: Fuente y Fonda
places.note: Grandmother-style cooking; humita and other criollo comfort dishes in big portions.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Stalls sell humitas and tamales to take away when the corn is in season.

food.name: Tomatican
food.desc: Cuyo skillet stew of tomato, onion, corn and beef bound with egg, a frugal harvest dish that still turns up on old-school Mendoza menus.

places.name: Fuente y Fonda
places.note: One of the few city kitchens still cooking the old Cuyano home recipes.

places.name: Siete Cocinas
places.note: Chef-driven regional menu that revives Cuyo dishes like tomatican and charqui.

places.name: La Marchigiana
places.note: Family restaurant since 1950 mixing Italian-Argentine staples with local classics.

food.name: Chivo asado
food.desc: Young goat from Malargue, splayed on an iron cross over embers until the skin crackles. Mendoza's great special-occasion roast.

places.name: Siete Cocinas
places.note: Reliable city address for Malargue goat if you cannot get to the south of the province.

places.name: Don Mario
places.note: Traditional parrilla that puts chivo on the grill alongside the usual beef cuts.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Butchers sell whole chivo here and nearby comedores cook it at lunchtime.

food.name: Malbec
food.desc: The high-altitude red that made Mendoza famous, grown from Lujan de Cuyo up to the cool Uco Valley. Tasting rooms sit minutes from the centre.

places.name: Bodega Los Toneles
places.note: Restored 1922 winery inside the city with tastings and a well-regarded restaurant.

places.name: The Vines of Mendoza tasting room
places.note: Central tasting room pouring flights from small Uco Valley producers.

places.name: Azafran
places.note: Restaurant with a walk-in cellar; the sommelier matches bottles to your order.

food.name: Fernet con Coca
food.desc: Bitter Italian amaro poured long over ice with cola. The default Argentine night-out drink, mixed strong and shared from the bottle.

places.name: Por Aca
places.note: Loud student-favourite bar on the main going-out strip, open late.

places.name: Antares
places.note: Argentine craft-beer chain with a Mendoza branch; good for a mixed round.

places.name: Aristides Villanueva bar strip
places.note: Ten blocks of terraces where the city drinks; every bar pours it by the tall glass.

landmarks: Parque General San Martín
A magnificent 971-acre park designed by Carlos Thays, its rose gardens, rowing lake, and forested avenues form the green lungs of wine-country Mendoza.
Cerro de la Gloria
Crowned by a dramatic bronze monument to San Martín's Army of the Andes, this hilltop delivers sweeping views over the city and distant cordillera.
Plaza Independencia
Mendoza's grand central square hosts illuminated fountains, artisan fairs, and shady acacias, anchoring the four satellite plazas of the earthquake-rebuilt city grid.
Luján de Cuyo and Maipú Wineries
The historic bodegas ringing the city, from Trapiche to Catena Zapata, pour Argentina's finest Malbec against a backdrop of vineyards and snowcapped Andes.
Ruinas de San Francisco (Área Fundacional)
Earthquake-shattered walls of a Jesuit-Franciscan church mark Mendoza's original 1561 foundation site, alongside a museum preserving the buried colonial city.
Plaza España
The prettiest of Mendoza's plazas dazzles with Andalusian tilework, a fountain, and murals celebrating the bonds between Spain and Argentina.
Termas de Cacheuta
Steaming thermal pools terraced above the Mendoza River canyon offer a soothing mountain spa escape just an hour from the city.
Portones del Parque
Ornate wrought-iron gates crowned with a condor, shipped from Britain in 1907, form the triumphal entrance to Parque San Martín and a classic photo stop.
Teatro Independencia
Mendoza's premier opera house on Plaza Independencia, opened in the 1920s and still the city's main venue for theater and classical performances.
Museo del Pasado Cuyano
A 19th-century mansion just off Plaza Independencia holding General San Martín memorabilia and artifacts from Mendoza's colonial and independence-era past.

train.note: Mendoza has had no long-distance passenger train since the Buenos Aires service was cut in the 1990s, and the Transandine railway over the Andes to Chile has been closed since 1984, so there is no rail option in or out of the city. The only track in use is the Metrotranvia, an urban light-rail line running through Mendoza between Maipu and Las Heras, which is city transport rather than intercity travel. Trenes Argentinos (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/transporte/trenes-argentinos) runs long-distance trains only out of Buenos Aires, and the nearest railhead on that network is Justo Daract in San Luis province, still several hours away by bus. Argentina's one international train, Posadas-Encarnacion for Paraguay, is on the far side of the country.

bus.note: Everything leaves from the Terminal de Omnibus de Mendoza, known as the Terminal del Sol, in Guaymallen just east of the centre and walkable from downtown. Domestic coaches run to Buenos Aires (13-15 hours, overnight cama services are the norm), Cordoba, San Juan, Bariloche and San Rafael. The international run to Santiago de Chile crosses the Andes by the Cristo Redentor / Los Libertadores pass in roughly 7-9 hours, including a slow joint Argentina-Chile border post at Los Libertadores where every bag comes off the bus - do not carry fresh fruit, meat or plants, which Chile confiscates. In winter (roughly June to September) heavy snow can close the pass for a day or more, so keep your onward plans flexible.

ferry.note: Mendoza lies in the Andean foothills about 1,000 km from the Atlantic, so there are no ferry services.
